chunks: "The poles are the magnetic poles on the rotor: the permanent magnets arranged north, south, north, south around the rim.
Magnets come in pairs, so a 14-pole motor has seven pole pairs.
This matters because the electrical cycle is tied to pole pairs: one full mechanical rotation produces p electrical cycles, so electrical frequency is p times rpm over 60.

How it affects performance: more poles means the stator field only has to rotate a fraction of a turn for each electrical cycle, so for the same motor size you get more torque at lower speed, because the magnetic path through the back-iron can be thinner and the winding end-turns are shorter.
That's why gimbal motors and drone outrunners have lots of poles, around 12 to 14 or more.
You also get finer position resolution, since the Hall code changes every 60^ degrees over p of shaft angle. The cost is a higher electrical frequency for the same rpm.
A 14-pole motor at 30 000 rpm is at 3.
5 kilohertz electrical, so the inverter has to commutate at 21 kilohertz in six-step, iron loss and switching loss go up, and the controller loop needs enough bandwidth.
A 2-pole motor can spin very fast with a low electrical frequency, which is why high-speed spindles and turbo-machinery often use few poles.
Pole count also interacts with the slot count to set cogging, so I'd choose a good combination, like 12 slots and 14 poles."
